paper_title: PN-Mix: Pair-Norm Guided Mixed-Precision Key Cache Quantization for Efficient Long-Output LLM Inference

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. Through attention logit perturbation analysis at the RoPE channel-pair level, we show that quantization errors in channel pairs with large query--key pair-norm products contribute significantly to logit variation. Based on this insight, we propose PN-Mix, a mixed-precision key-cache quantization method for RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, which allocates higher precision to salient channel pairs identified once during the prefill stage and reused throughout decoding. Across standard reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix with 2.26-bit average precision achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32--2.39 bits. Furthermore, in our Pareto sweep, PN-Mix degrades gracefully down to 1.5 bits, whereas the compared baselines exhibit sharper performance drops below 2.25 bits.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Long-output inference has become central capability of large language models (LLMs), enabling applications that require extended generation such as code generation and complex problem solving. However, long-output decoding exposes severe systems bottleneck in the key-value (KV) cache, which stores previous keys and values but grows linearly with sequence length and batch size. This growth increases memory pressure, reducing the feasible batch size for serving and limiting the maximum generation length. KV cache quantization alleviates this bottleneck by storing cached keys and values at lower precision while retaining all token positions and the original cache structure. Yet this compression is inherently lossy: aggressive low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) can introduce errors that substantially degrade reasoning accuracy over long chains of thought (Liu et al., 2025). Thus, effective KV cache quantization requires not only lowering precision, but also allocating the limited bit budget to the most critical components. Recent mixed-precision methods allocate higher precision to salient key channels, motivated by the greater quantization sensitivity of keys than values (Li et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026; Hariri et al., 2026). However, their saliency estimates rely on key statistics alone and operate at the individualchannel level, overlooking querykey interactions and the channel-pair structure induced by RoPE. adjacent channel pairs. As result, PN-Mix remains input-adaptive without offline calibration and avoids repeated saliency recomputation during decoding. sections.content: We provide brief overview of the attention and online KV-cache quantization setup used in this work. For decoder-layer hidden state RT with sequence length and hidden dimension D, Grouped Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023) projects into RHT and K, RH kvT d, where H, kv, and denote the number of query heads, KV heads, and the head dimension. RoPE (Su et al., 2024) gives Qh,t = Qh,tRt and Kh,t = Kh,tRt, where Rt is position-dependent block-diagonal rotation over Prior work has explored several directions for reducing KV cache memory, including token eviction (Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2025), low-rank approximation (Chang et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025), merging (Zhang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024), pruning (Xu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), and quantization. Among them, KV cache quantization reduces memory by lowering the representation precision of cached tensors while retaining the cache structure. We focus on KV cache quantization, which can be broadly divided into uniform-precision and mixed-precision approaches.

sections.title: 4 Preliminary Analysis
sections.content: Uniform-precision KV cache quantization assigns the same bit-width to all quantized cache elements. Prior methods reduce low-bit quantization error through key/value-specific grouping (Liu et al., 2024), distribution-aware quantization (Hooper et al., 2024), residual correction (Kang et al., 2024), outlier-token preservation (Su et al., 2025a), Walsh Hadamard channel rotations (Su et al., 2025b), projection-based 1-bit sign quantization (Zandieh et al., 2025), and polar-coordinate quantization of RoPE channel pairs (Wu et al., 2025). However, because they assign the same bit-width regardless of cache-element sensitivity, uniform-precision methods may insufficiently control errors in important components, which can accumulate over long chains of thought in reasoning models (Liu et al., 2025).

sections.title: 3.2 Mixed-Precision Quantization
sections.content: Mixed-precision quantization instead allocates limited bit budget according to estimated importance. Existing methods differ in allocation granularity, including token-level (Yang et al., 2024), layer-level (Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026), and channel-level allocation. Since key-cache quantization importance is highly non-uniform across channels due to channel-wise outliers (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024), recent channel-level methods focus on assigning higher precision to salient key channels. ChanMix (Liao and Wen, 2026) uses an offline calibration set to identify retrieval-head channels, assigns them 4-bit precision, and allocates 3/2/1-bit precision to the remaining channels via minmax range-based clustering. Kitty (Xia et al., 2026) dynamically re-estimates channel saliency for each quantization group using average key magnitude, assigning 4-bit precision to salient channels and 2-bit precision to the rest. Although these methods improve over uniform precision, they estimate saliency from alone and assign precision at the individual-channel level. This misses two structures that directly affect attention: attention logits are determined by the interaction between and K, and RoPE couples channels into pairs. In contrast, PN-Mix estimates saliency from querykey interactions at the RoPE channelpair level and allocates mixed precision to the key cache accordingly. To achieve accuracy-preserving 2.25-bit KVcache compression for long-output inference, we investigate three design questions: (1) which cache (key or value) to refine; (2) how to define an importance score for assigning higher precision within the key cache; and (3) how to exploit this importance score efficiently during long-output inference. We examine these questions sequentially and use the resulting observations to guide our mixedprecision key-cache quantization design.

sections.content: Under 2.25-bit budget1, prior work indicates the key cache is more sensitive to quantization than the value cache (Li et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026). We verify this by quantizing either or to 2.25 bits and comparing against an FP16 baseline on AIME datasets. We evaluate DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama8B (R1-Llama-8B) and Qwen3-8B, generating up to 32K tokens per response. Accounting for attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2024), we also evaluate variants preserving the initial 32 tokens in FP16, following prior work (Xia et al., 2026). Table 8 shows that -only quantization causes less degradation than K-only quantization, even without sink-token protection. While preserving the first 32 tokens in FP16 improves both, -only quantization approaches the FP16 baseline whereas K-only quantization still exhibits non-negligible degradation. These results lead to two design choices. First, sink tokens should be preserved in full precision for both caches. Second, key-cache quantization should be refined more carefully than value-cache quantization under low-bit compression.

Figure 2 summarizes the results, with full simulation details provided in Appendix B. As shown in Figure 2, the proposed K pair norm achieves the lowest DA KL among all compared mixed-precision criteria on both models, indicating better preservation of the attention distribution under the same effective bit budget. Its improvement over the pair norm further indicates that incorporating query-side information provides additional benefit beyond accounting for the RoPE channel-pair structure alone. Based on these results, we use σh,i in Eq. 5 as the importance score for mixed-precision key-cache quantization. With σh,i established as the importance score, the remaining challenge is to estimate it efficiently during long-output inference. ChanMix relies on offline profiling, eliminating online selection overhead but sacrificing input-adaptive channel allocation, whereas Kitty performs input-adaptive selection for each quantization group. However, this requires repeatedly identifying salient channels and storing separate set of channel indices for each group. As decoding proceeds and more groups accumulate, the resulting index storage and loading overhead can grow substantially. To retain input-adaptive importance while avoiding repeated salient-pair selection and index management during long decoding, we choose to compute σh,i once from the prefill tokens and reuse the selected channel pairs throughout decoding. For this prefill-only strategy to be effective, the prefill-based importance score should satisfy two properties. First, it should be predictive: channel pairs identified as important during prefill should remain salient throughout subsequent decoding. Second, it should be selective: the importance should be concentrated on subset of channel pairs so that assigning higher precision to the selected pairs remains effective under limited bit budget. We first evaluate the predictiveness of prefillbased selection by comparing its quantization quality against full-sequence oracle that computes importance scores using the complete sequence. Using the same H3(50%)L1 simulation setup as in 4.2, Figure 2 shows that the prefill-based K pair norm achieves DA KL close to its full-sequence counterpart on both evaluated models. To further understand why prefill-based selection remains effective, Appendix compares the channel pairs identified from prefill with those that are salient during decoding. Among the evaluated criteria, the prefill-based K pair norm yields the highest average Jaccard overlap with decoding-time salient pairs. Moreover, Appendix shows that this overlap does not systematically decrease as decoding progresses, including in long-generation and multi-topic settings. We next examine selectivity. Approximately 97 99% of the total importance is concentrated in the top 50% of channel pairs (Figure 5); these values denote the median across layers, KV heads, and prompts. Together, these results indicate that σh,i can be computed once during the input prefill stage and that the selected channel pairs can be reused throughout long-output decoding.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented PN-Mix, pair-norm-based mixedprecision key-cache quantization method for RoPEbased decoder-only LLMs, designed to support efficient long-output inference. PN-Mix allocates higher precision to RoPE channel pairs with large querykey pair-norm products and estimates these salient pairs once during prefill, avoiding offline calibration and repeated decoding-time saliency recomputation. Across standard reasoning, code generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision baselines with lower average keycache precision. It also remains robust in the sub2.25-bit regime and expands the feasible serving region for long-output inference.

sections.content: PN-Mix is most directly applicable to RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, as its saliency score is defined over RoPE channel pairs. sections.content: Figure 6 evaluates how peak GPU memory and generation throughput scale with generation length and operations during decoding. The kernels are implemented for the configuration used in our downstream task evaluation, namely bH = 3, bL = 1, and bV = 2. After mixedprecision quantization of the key cache, salient channel pairs are represented by integers in the range [0, 7], while the remaining channels are represented by integers in the range [0, 1]. Since the least significant 1 bit is shared by all channels and the upper 2 bits are meaningful only for salient channel pairs, our implementation packs these two parts into separate uint8 tensors. Specifically, we first extract the LSBs of all channels and pack every 8 consecutive token values of each channel into one byte, producing packed_low, which is stored for all channels. We then extract the upper 2 bits and pack every 4 consecutive token values of each channel into one byte, producing packed_hi, which is stored only for the salient channel pairs. For the value cache, after quantization, every 4 consecutive channel values of each token are packed into one byte and stored as uint8 tensor. h,1:t/ During the decoding-stage attention computation, we launch two Triton kernels: one for computing Qh,t and the other for computing Ah,tVh,1:t. Each kernel sequentially processes the sink-token region, the quantized-cache region, and the residual-buffer region. For the quantized region, the dequantized key or value cache is never written back to global memory. Instead, each quantization group is loaded into on-chip registers, dequantized, and immediately consumed by the dotproduct computation. Average Key Bit-Width Calculation and Method Configurations To compare the methods under similar key-cache memory budget, we include both the quantized key values and the additional metadata required by each method in the bit-width calculation. Since the methods use different native precision-allocation schemes, Tables 2 and 3 retain these schemes and use configurations within narrow 2.252.4-bit range rather than enforcing an exact bit match. The resulting comparison therefore focuses on accuracy preservation in this low-bit regime rather than on the best-performing or recommended operating point of each method. Figure 7: Per-step decode latency on single A100SXM4-40GB GPU. We measure Qwen3-8B decode latency with Kitty and PN-Mix. The shaded region (steps 11K31K) indicates the KV-cache-readdominated regime, and β denotes the linear-regression slope in this region (µs/step). These results distinguish two deployment regimes. When GPU memory is sufficient for the desired batch size and generation length, FP16 provides higher same-batch throughput because it avoids quantization and dequantization overhead. In memory-bound settings with larger batches or longer generations, PN-Mix can run configurations that exceed the FP16 memory limit. This larger feasible batch size allows PN-Mix to achieve higher maximum per-GPU throughput under the same memory budget. Per-Step Decoding Latency Analysis Figure 7 compares the per-step decoding latency of PN-Mix and Kitty along long-CoT trajectory with = 1, = 141, and Lgen = 32K, measured using torch.cuda.Event. Both methods remain at roughly 4548 ms plateau up to approximately 10K decoding steps. Beyond this point, per-step latency increases steadily with the growing KVcache length. Over the linear region from 11K to 31K steps, PN-Mix exhibits lower latency-growth slope than Kitty (2.17 vs. 2.38 µs/step), corresponding to an 8.8% reduction. At 32K decoding steps, PN-Mix is also 6.8 ms faster than Kitty. These results show that PN-Mixs lower average key-cache bit-width and absence of page-wise salient-channel index I/O lead to practical decoding latency improvements.
